strengths.title: Addresses a genuine gap in parsing technology
strengths.description: UCCA's conjunction of reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes is not supported by existing parsers. The paper clearly identifies this gap and provides a working solution, which is a meaningful contribution to the semantic parsing literature.
evidence: Literature review in Section 6 confirms that existing parsers (DAGParser, TurboParser, UPARSE, MaltParser, LSTM Parser) support subsets but not the full conjunction
Conversion experiments (Section 4, Table 2) demonstrate that baselines adapted to UCCA perform substantially worse, especially on remote edges

strengths.title: Well-motivated transition set design
strengths.description: The novel transitions (NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP) are clearly motivated by UCCA's structural properties. The transition set is well-documented with explicit conditions (Figure 2) and handles the key challenges of DAG parsing.
evidence: Section 3 provides clear definitions of each transition with preconditions and effects
Transitions directly address the three key challenges: NODE for non-terminals, EDGE/REMOTE for reentrancy, SWAP for discontinuity
Design follows established patterns from prior work on dependency graph parsing and constituency parsing

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation
strengths.description: The paper includes in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation, multiple baseline comparisons (via conversion), ablation studies across three classifier variants, and reporting of both primary and remote edge performance. The evaluation methodology is thorough.
evidence: Table 2 reports results on both Wiki (in-domain) and 20K Leagues (out-of-domain) test sets
Comparison to six baseline parsers with conversion procedures and upper bounds
Ablation across TUPASparse, TUPAMLP, and TUPABiLSTM shows impact of classifier architecture

strengths.title: Strong empirical results on remote edges
strengths.description: TUPA achieves 49.4% F-score on remote edges in-domain, compared to 1–3.7% for baseline DAG parsers. This is a substantial improvement and demonstrates the effectiveness of the transition set design for handling reentrancy.
evidence: Table 2: TUPABiLSTM remote F-score (49.4%) is order of magnitude higher than DAGParser (1%) and TurboParser (3.7%)
Results section (line 615): 'this in itself cannot account for their poor performance on remote edges, which is an order of magnitude lower than that of TUPABiLSTM'
Remote edge performance is critical for evaluating DAG parsing capability

strengths.title: Clear presentation and reproducibility
strengths.description: The paper is well-written with clear explanations of UCCA, the transition set, and the experimental setup. The authors promise to release code and models, supporting reproducibility.
evidence: Section 2 provides clear introduction to UCCA with motivating examples (Figures 1a–c)
Section 3 systematically introduces the transition set with Figure 2 showing all transitions and conditions
Footnote 1: 'Our code and models will be made freely available upon publication'
Appendices provide hyperparameter details (Appendix C) and conversion procedures (Appendix D)

strengths.title: Appropriate use of dynamic oracle training
strengths.description: The paper employs dynamic oracle training (Goldberg and Nivre, 2012), which is well-suited to transition-based parsing with complex transition sets. This is a principled approach to handling the non-determinism in the oracle.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 360–380): 'For training the transition classifiers, we use a dynamic oracle (Goldberg and Nivre, 2012), i.e., an oracle that outputs a set of optimal transitions'
Dynamic oracle allows multiple valid transitions at each step, reducing training bias from greedy oracle decisions

concerns.title: Novelty is primarily application-driven rather than algorithmic
concerns.description: The core contribution is applying existing transition-based parsing techniques to a new semantic representation scheme (UCCA). The individual components (transition-based parsing, BiLSTM feature representation, dynamic oracle training) are well-established. The novelty lies in the combination and the specific transition set design, which is incremental.
evidence: Transition-based parsing established by Nivre (2003) and extensively developed in dependency parsing literature
BiLSTM feature representation follows Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016) and Dyer et al. (2015)
Dynamic oracle training from Goldberg and Nivre (2012)
Novel transitions (NODE, REMOTE) are adaptations of existing transitions from prior work on constituency and dependency graph parsing
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Frame the contribution more explicitly as a novel application of transition-based parsing to UCCA, rather than claiming fundamental algorithmic innovation. Emphasize the engineering contribution and the specific design choices for UCCA.

concerns.title: Generalization claims lack empirical support
concerns.description: The paper claims the transition set and approach generalize to other semantic DAG structures and languages with discontinuous constituents (Abstract, Conclusion). However, no experiments on other DAG structures (AMR, SDP) or non-English languages are provided. The claim is prospective and speculative.
evidence: Abstract: 'its ability to handle more general graph structures will inform the development of parsers for other semantic DAG structures'
Conclusion: 'Our contribution to this literature is a general grammarless parser that supports multiple parents, discontinuous units and non-terminal nodes'
No experiments on AMR, SDP, or other languages despite mentioning them in related work (Section 6)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either provide empirical validation on at least one other DAG structure (e.g., AMR or SDP) or reframe the generalization claim as a future direction. Acknowledge that the transition set is currently UCCA-specific and may require adaptation for other schemes.

concerns.title: BiLSTM superiority confounded with feature representation
concerns.description: The comparison between TUPASparse, TUPAMLP, and TUPABiLSTM conflates two factors: (1) the classifier architecture (sparse perceptron vs. feedforward NN vs. BiLSTM) and (2) the feature representation (sparse vs. dense embeddings). No controlled ablation isolates the contribution of each factor.
evidence: Section 3: TUPASparse uses sparse features; TUPAMLP and TUPABiLSTM use dense embeddings
Table 2: TUPABiLSTM (73.5% F-score) substantially outperforms TUPASparse (64.1%) and TUPAMLP (64.9%)
No ablation study with sparse features + BiLSTM or dense embeddings + perceptron to isolate contributions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablation studies isolating the contribution of: (1) dense embeddings vs. sparse features, (2) BiLSTM architecture vs. feedforward NN, (3) hyperparameter tuning differences. This would clarify whether the improvement is due to the architecture or the feature representation.

concerns.title: Greedy inference may be suboptimal; no beam search comparison
concerns.description: The paper uses greedy inference for all classifiers, without comparison to beam search or globally normalized models. Greedy decoding can accumulate errors, especially for complex DAG structures. Beam search might recover 2–5% F-score.
evidence: Section 3 (line 340): 'For all classifiers, inference is performed greedily, i.e., without beam search.'
Section 4 (line 599): 'DAGParser and UPARSE use beam search by default, with a beam size of 5 and 4 respectively.'
No comparison with beam search or globally normalized models (e.g., Andor et al., 2016)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement beam search for TUPABiLSTM and report results with different beam sizes (e.g., 1, 4, 8). Compare with globally normalized models if feasible. This would clarify whether greedy inference is a limitation.

concerns.title: Dynamic oracle completeness not formally proven
concerns.description: The paper uses a dynamic oracle for training but provides only a 'proof sketch' in Appendix E. If the oracle is incomplete (i.e., does not always find a path to the gold graph), training will be suboptimal. Formal completeness proof is missing.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 360–380): 'For training the transition classifiers, we use a dynamic oracle (Goldberg and Nivre, 2012)'
Footnote in Section 3: 'See Appendix E for a proof sketch for the completeness'
Appendix E contains only a 'proof sketch', not a formal proof
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a formal proof of oracle completeness or reference a published proof. If completeness cannot be proven, discuss the implications for training and report oracle coverage statistics (percentage of states where a valid transition exists).

concerns.title: Conversion procedures introduce confounds in baseline comparison
concerns.description: Baseline parsers are compared via conversion to bilexical graphs and trees, which introduces information loss (upper bounds: 91% for bilexical graphs, 100% for trees). Baselines are not hyperparameter-tuned on converted data and use default settings. This makes the comparison indirect and potentially unfair.
evidence: Section 4 (lines 540–570): 'As no direct comparison with existing parsers is possible, we compare TUPA to bilexical dependency graph parsers... To facilitate the comparison, we convert our training set into bilexical graphs.'
Section 4 (line 599): 'Default settings are used in all cases.'
Table 2: Upper bound for bilexical graph conversion is 91% (primary), 58.3% (remote)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: If possible, retrain baseline parsers on UCCA-native representations or provide more detailed analysis of how conversion affects each baseline. Alternatively, acknowledge the limitation more explicitly and discuss how it affects the interpretation of results.

concerns.title: Inter-annotator agreement baseline not re-measured on current test set
concerns.description: The paper cites inter-annotator agreement (80–85% F-score) from Abend and Rappoport (2013) but does not re-measure it on the current test set. The cited agreement may not be directly comparable to TUPA's performance on the same test set.
evidence: Section 5 (lines 610–612): 'Its performance in absolute terms, of 73.5% F-score on primary edges, is encouraging in light of UCCA's inter-annotator agreement of 80–85% F-score on them (Abend and Rappoport, 2013).'
No re-measurement of inter-annotator agreement on Wiki or 20K Leagues test sets
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-measure inter-annotator agreement on the current test set (or at least on a sample) to ensure comparability. Alternatively, discuss the potential differences between the cited agreement and the current test set.

concerns.title: No error analysis or systematic failure mode investigation
concerns.description: The paper reports aggregate F-scores but does not analyze error types, systematic failure modes, or how TUPA's errors relate to inter-annotator disagreement. This limits understanding of where the parser struggles and whether 73.5% F-score is acceptable for downstream applications.
evidence: Results section (lines 601–699) reports only aggregate metrics (precision, recall, F-score)
No breakdown of errors by phenomenon (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes)
No analysis of whether TUPA's errors align with inter-annotator disagreement patterns
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide error analysis breaking down performance by structural phenomenon (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes). Compare TUPA's errors to inter-annotator disagreement patterns. Discuss specific failure cases and their implications for downstream applications.

concerns.title: Ratio feature contribution not isolated via ablation
concerns.description: The paper introduces a novel real-valued feature (ratio of terminals to nodes) as a regularizer for node creation. However, no ablation study demonstrates its contribution to TUPA's performance.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 350–360): 'Finally, for all classifiers we add a novel real-valued feature to the input vector, ratio, corresponding to the ratio between the number of terminals to number of nodes in the graph G. This feature serves as a regularizer for the creation of new nodes.'
No ablation study removing the ratio feature to measure its impact
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide an ablation study showing TUPA's performance with and without the ratio feature. This would clarify whether the feature is beneficial and generalizable to other parsing tasks.

concerns.title: Discarded edges and nodes may affect evaluation
concerns.description: The paper discards inter-sentence edges (0.18%), linkage nodes, and implicit nodes during preprocessing. These discarded elements may be important for downstream applications, and their removal may artificially inflate parser performance.
evidence: Section 4 (lines 520–530): 'While UCCA edges can cross sentence boundaries, we adhere to the common practice in semantic parsing and train our parsers on individual sentences, discarding inter-relations between them (0.18% of the edges). We also discard linkage nodes and edges (as they often express inter-sentence relations and are thus mostly redundant when applied at the sentence level) as well as implicit nodes.'
No analysis of impact of discarding these elements
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate TUPA on the full UCCA representation including inter-sentence edges, linkage nodes, and implicit nodes. Report performance with and without these elements to assess their impact.

concerns.title: Transition set design is UCCA-specific; generalization unclear
concerns.description: The transition set distinguishes between primary and remote edges, which is specific to UCCA's annotation scheme. Other DAG structures (AMR, SDP) use different edge types and may not have this distinction. Adaptation to other schemes would require redesign.
evidence: Section 3: LEFT-EDGE/RIGHT-EDGE create primary edges; LEFT-REMOTE/RIGHT-REMOTE create remote edges

Section 2 (lines 200–210): 'One incoming edge for each non-root node is marked as primary, and the rest (mostly used for implicit relations and arguments) as remote edges, a distinction made by the annotator.'
Section 6 discusses AMR and SDP but does not address how to adapt TUPA's transitions to these schemes
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss how the transition set would need to be adapted for other DAG structures. Provide concrete examples of how transitions would differ for AMR or SDP. This would clarify the generalizability of the approach.

comparable_works.citation_label: Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Directly relevant: BiLSTM feature representation for transition-based parsing
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TUPA uses the same BiLSTM architecture as Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016) for feature representation. The novelty is in applying this architecture to UCCA parsing with a new transition set, not in the feature representation itself.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3 (line 340): 'Finally, TUPABiLSTM uses a bidirectional LSTM for feature representation, on top of the dense embedding features, an architecture similar to Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016).'

comparable_works.citation_label: Dyer et al. (2015)
comparable_works.relevance: Directly relevant: Stack LSTM-based transition-based parsing
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Dyer et al. (2015) introduced stack LSTM for transition-based parsing. TUPA uses BiLSTM (not stack LSTM) but follows a similar neural architecture paradigm. TUPA's contribution is in the transition set design, not the neural architecture.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 1 (lines 101–115): 'We are further motivated by the strength of transition-based methods in related tasks, including dependency parsing (Dyer et al., 2015; Andor et al., 2016; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016).'

comparable_works.citation_label: Sagae and Tsujii (2008), Ribeyre et al. (2014), Tokgöz and Eryiğit (2015)
comparable_works.relevance: Directly relevant: Transition-based dependency graph parsing
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These works introduced transition-based parsing for DAGs with multiple parents. TUPA adapts their techniques (e.g., leaving stack unchanged for edge transitions) to UCCA. The novelty is in the specific transition set for UCCA's properties (discontinuity, non-terminal nodes).
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3 (lines 301–320): 'To support the prediction of multiple parents, node and edge transitions leave the stack unchanged, as in other work on transition-based dependency graph parsing (Sagae and Tsujii, 2008; Ribeyre et al., 2014; Tokgöz and Eryiğit, 2015).'

comparable_works.citation_label: Maier (2015), Maier and Lichte (2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Directly relevant: Transition-based constituency parsing with discontinuous constituents
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Maier (2015) introduced the SWAP transition for handling discontinuous constituents. TUPA adopts this transition for UCCA. The novelty is in combining SWAP with other transitions (NODE, REMOTE) for UCCA's specific properties.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3 (lines 301–320): 'To handle discontinuous nodes, SWAP pops the second node on the stack and adds it to the top of the buffer, as with the similarly named transition in previous work (Nivre, 2009; Maier, 2015).'

comparable_works.citation_label: Goldberg and Nivre (2012)
comparable_works.relevance: Directly relevant: Dynamic oracle training for transition-based parsing
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TUPA uses dynamic oracle training from Goldberg and Nivre (2012) without modification. This is a standard technique, not a novel contribution.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3 (lines 360–380): 'For training the transition classifiers, we use a dynamic oracle (Goldberg and Nivre, 2012), i.e., an oracle that outputs a set of optimal transitions.'

comparable_works.citation_label: Flanigan et al. (2014), Damonte et al. (2017), Zhou et al. (2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Related: Transition-based AMR parsing
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These works address transition-based parsing for AMR, another semantic DAG structure. TUPA differs in that it handles UCCA's specific properties (non-terminal nodes, primary/remote edge distinction). The paper argues that existing AMR parsers cannot handle arbitrary DAGs due to node removal before parent prediction.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 6 (lines 700–799): 'Furthermore, existing transition-based AMR parsers are not general DAG parsers. They are only able to predict a subset of reentrancies and discontinuities, as they may remove nodes before their parents have been predicted (Damonte et al., 2017).'

comparable_works.citation_label: Oepen et al. (2014, 2015) - Semantic Dependency Parsing
comparable_works.relevance: Related: Broad-coverage semantic dependency parsing (SDP)
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SDP addresses similar phenomena (reentrancy, discontinuity) but uses bilexical dependencies without non-terminal nodes. TUPA extends SDP-like parsing to support non-terminal nodes, which is a key difference.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 6 (lines 700–799): 'Most closely related to this work is Broad-Coverage Semantic Dependency Parsing (SDP), addressed in two SemEval tasks (Oepen et al., 2014, 2015). Like UCCA parsing, SDP addresses a wide range of semantic phenomena, and supports discontinuous units and reentrancy. However, SDP uses bilexical dependencies, disallowing non-terminal nodes.'

uncertainty_flags: Claim of 'first parser' relies on literature review; no exhaustive survey of all parsers documented
Transition-based approach motivated by conceptual similarity, not empirical proof of optimality; no comparison with graph-based or grammar-based alternatives
BiLSTM superiority confounded with feature representation (sparse vs. dense embeddings); no controlled ablation isolating architecture contribution
Greedy inference used; no comparison with beam search or globally normalized models
Dynamic oracle completeness not formally proven; Appendix E contains only a 'proof sketch'
Conversion procedures introduce information loss; baselines may be unfairly disadvantaged; no direct comparison on shared representation
Evaluation metric (yield-based edge matching) not validated against downstream application needs
Test sets (Wiki, 20K Leagues) may be small or unrepresentative; no cross-lingual evaluation
Discarded edges (inter-sentence, linkage, implicit) may be important for downstream applications
Hyperparameter tuning on development set; potential overfitting to Wiki corpus
Generalization claim to other DAG structures and languages is prospective, not empirically validated
Ratio feature contribution not isolated via ablation study
Inter-annotator agreement (80–85%) cited from prior work, not re-measured on current test set
Error analysis and systematic failure modes not discussed; unclear if 73.5% F-score is acceptable for downstream applications
Transition set is UCCA-specific (primary vs. remote edge distinction); unclear how to adapt to other schemes
alternative_interpretations: The contribution could be framed as a novel engineering solution to a specific problem (UCCA parsing) rather than a fundamental algorithmic innovation. This would lower novelty expectations but clarify the actual contribution.
BiLSTM's superiority might be due to better hyperparameter tuning rather than architectural advantages. A controlled ablation with equal tuning effort would test this.

The poor performance of baseline parsers via conversion might reflect suboptimal conversion procedures rather than fundamental limitations of those parsers. Direct comparison on UCCA-native representations would be more conclusive.

The 73.5% F-score might be acceptable for some downstream applications (e.g., machine translation evaluation) but not others (e.g., semantic role labeling). Without downstream evaluation, it's unclear whether the performance is sufficient.
The transition set might not generalize to other DAG structures due to UCCA-specific design choices (e.g., primary/remote edge distinction). Generalization claims should be more cautious.
Greedy inference might be sufficient for UCCA parsing despite being suboptimal in other tasks. Beam search comparison would clarify this.
The dynamic oracle might be incomplete for UCCA's transition set, but the impact on training might be negligible. Oracle coverage statistics would clarify this.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about its methods, data, and evaluation. Hyperparameter details are provided in Appendix C, and conversion procedures are described in Appendix D.
The paper acknowledges limitations of the conversion procedures (upper bounds reported) and discusses why baseline parsers perform poorly on remote edges.
However, the paper could be more transparent about the confounds in the BiLSTM vs. sparse/feedforward comparison and the lack of beam search comparison.
The generalization claims in the Abstract and Conclusion are somewhat overstated relative to the empirical evidence. The paper would benefit from more cautious framing of these claims.
The paper does not discuss potential negative results or limitations of the transition-based approach (e.g., why not graph-based parsing?).
The paper promises to release code and models, which supports reproducibility and transparency.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The contribution is primarily an application of existing techniques (transition-based parsing, BiLSTM feature representation, dynamic oracle training) to a new semantic representation scheme (UCCA). While the specific transition set design is novel for UCCA, the individual components are well-established. The novelty is incremental but meaningful: it fills a gap in parsing technology for UCCA and demonstrates that transition-based parsing can handle the conjunction of reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes. However, the contribution is not a fundamental algorithmic or theoretical innovation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper demonstrated that the transition set generalizes to other DAG structures (AMR, SDP) with minimal adaptation, the novelty would be higher.
If the paper provided a formal proof of dynamic oracle completeness or showed that oracle incompleteness has negligible impact, the methodological rigor would be stronger.
If the paper compared with beam search or globally normalized models and showed that greedy inference is sufficient, the evaluation would be more convincing.
If the paper provided controlled ablations isolating the contribution of BiLSTM architecture from feature representation, the claims about neural architectures would be more credible.
If the paper evaluated TUPA on downstream applications (machine translation, semantic role labeling) and showed that 73.5% F-score is sufficient, the practical impact would be clearer.

If the paper provided error analysis showing which phenomena (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes) are most challenging and how TUPA addresses them, the contribution would be better understood.

The novelty lies in the specific transition set design (NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP) for UCCA, which is an incremental extension of prior work on dependency graph parsing and constituency parsing.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes a solid incremental contribution by applying transition-based parsing to UCCA and demonstrating that it effectively handles the conjunction of reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes. The empirical results are strong, especially for remote edges, and the evaluation is comprehensive. However, the novelty is primarily application-driven rather than algorithmic, and generalization claims lack empirical support. Overall, this is a competent engineering contribution that fills a gap in parsing technology for UCCA, but it is not a fundamental innovation. The confidence interval reflects the solid but incremental nature of the contribution.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper introduces TUPA, a transition-based parser for UCCA that claims to be the first parser supporting the simultaneous conjunction of three structural properties: reentrancy (DAG structures), discontinuous constituents, and non-terminal nodes. The core contribution is a novel transition set (NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP) combined with BiLSTM-based feature representation. The work is methodologically sound and empirically thorough, with in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation, baseline comparisons via conversion procedures, and ablation across three classifier variants. From a disruptive-novelty lens, the paper occupies an interesting position: it addresses a genuine gap (no existing parser supports the full conjunction), but the innovation is primarily **engineering-driven composition** rather than a fundamentally new conceptual frame. The transition set combines established techniques (NODE from constituency parsing, REMOTE edges from graph parsing, SWAP from discontinuous parsing) in a novel configuration. The BiLSTM contribution is incremental relative to concurrent work (Kiperwasser & Goldberg 2016, Dyer et al. 2015). The paper's strength lies in **problem formulation and systematic execution**, not in disruptive conceptual innovation. However, this does not diminish its value: it solves a real problem and opens a new parsing task.
logical_argument_graph: UCCA exhibits three properties not simultaneously supported by existing parsers → TUPA is needed
Transition-based parsing is conceptually similar to UCCA's predicate-argument structure → transition-based approach is suitable
Novel transitions (NODE, REMOTE, SWAP) enable DAG parsing with discontinuity and non-terminals → transition set is well-motivated
BiLSTM outperforms sparse and feedforward classifiers (Table 2: 73.5% vs 64.1% and 64.9% F-score) → neural feature representation is superior
TUPA outperforms baselines converted to bilexical graphs/trees (Table 2: 73.5% vs 69.9% LSTM Parser on primary edges) → TUPA is effective
Performance gap to inter-annotator agreement (73.5% vs 80–85%) is acceptable → TUPA is practically useful
Transition set generalizes to other DAG structures and languages → contribution has broader impact (prospective, not empirically validated)

strengths.title: Well-motivated problem formulation with genuine gap
strengths.description: The paper identifies a real and specific gap: no existing parser simultaneously supports reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes. This is clearly articulated and well-justified through examples (Figures 1a–c). The problem is concrete and addresses a practical need for UCCA parsing.
evidence: Introduction clearly states the conjunction of properties is unsupported by existing parsers
Section 2 provides linguistic motivation and examples for each property
Related work (Section 6) confirms no prior parser addresses all three properties together

strengths.title: Systematic and comprehensive empirical evaluation
strengths.description: The evaluation is thorough: in-domain and out-of-domain test sets, ablation across three classifier variants, conversion procedures with upper bounds, and comparison to multiple baseline parsers. This multi-faceted approach strengthens confidence in the results.
evidence: Table 2 reports results for 6 baseline parsers (DAGParser, TurboParser, UPARSE, MaltParser, LSTM Parser) and 3 TUPA variants
Upper bounds reported for conversion procedures (58.3% for bilexical graphs, 100% for trees)
Out-of-domain evaluation on 20K Leagues corpus shows generalization (73.5% → 68.6% on primary edges)
Ablation across TUPASparse, TUPAMLP, TUPABiLSTM isolates classifier contribution

strengths.title: Novel transition set design addressing specific structural challenges
strengths.description: The transition set (NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP) is well-designed to handle the three properties. The distinction between primary and remote edges is linguistically motivated and computationally sound. The SWAP transition for discontinuity and NODE for non-terminals are borrowed from prior work but combined in a novel way.
evidence: Figure 2 clearly specifies all 8 transitions with conditions
NODE transition creates non-terminal nodes (addressing non-terminal property)
LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE transitions enable reentrancy without primary-edge constraint (addressing reentrancy)
SWAP transition handles discontinuous nodes (addressing discontinuity)
Dynamic oracle training ensures reachability of gold graphs (Appendix E, proof sketch)

strengths.title: Strong empirical results on primary and remote edges
strengths.description: TUPA achieves 73.5% F-score on primary edges and 49.4% on remote edges (in-domain), substantially outperforming baselines. The remote-edge performance is particularly impressive: baselines achieve 1–3.7%, while TUPA achieves 49.4%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the transition set for handling reentrancy.
evidence: Table 2: TUPABiLSTM 73.5% primary (vs. 69.9% LSTM Parser), 49.4% remote (vs. 1–3.7% baselines)
Results section: 'TUPABiLSTM obtains substantially higher scores than TUPAMLP and all other parsers'
Out-of-domain performance (68.6% primary, 25.3% remote) shows robustness

strengths.title: Clear presentation and reproducibility
strengths.description: The paper is well-written with clear figures (Figures 1–5), explicit transition definitions (Figure 2), and detailed experimental setup (Section 4). Hyperparameters are reported in appendices. Code and models promised to be released. This facilitates reproducibility and future work.
evidence: Figure 2 provides complete transition set specification
Section 4 details data, implementation, and evaluation methodology
Appendix C contains hyperparameter values
Authors commit to releasing code and models upon publication

strengths.title: Thoughtful handling of conversion procedures and upper bounds
strengths.description: The paper acknowledges information loss from converting UCCA to bilexical graphs and trees, and reports upper bounds (58.3% for graphs, 100% for trees). This transparency allows readers to interpret baseline performance fairly and understand the limitations of indirect comparison.
evidence: Section 4: 'we compare TUPA to bilexical dependency graph parsers... To facilitate the comparison, we convert our training set into bilexical graphs'
Table 2: Upper bounds reported for all conversion procedures
Results section (lines 612–615): acknowledges that conversion upper bound (58.3%) does not fully explain baseline poor performance on remote edges

strengths.title: Practical utility demonstrated by performance relative to inter-annotator agreement
strengths.description: TUPA's 73.5% F-score on primary edges is reasonably close to inter-annotator agreement (80–85%), suggesting the parser may be useful for downstream applications. This provides a practical anchor for evaluating the significance of the results.
evidence: Results section (lines 610–612): 'Its performance in absolute terms, of 73.5% F-score on primary edges, is encouraging in light of UCCA's inter-annotator agreement of 80–85% F-score on them'
Gap of 6.5–11.5 percentage points is non-trivial but not prohibitive for some applications

concerns.title: Novelty claim is primarily engineering-driven composition, not disruptive conceptual innovation
concerns.description: The paper claims to introduce a 'first parser' for UCCA, which is true but narrow. The novelty is primarily in combining established techniques (NODE from constituency parsing, REMOTE edges from graph parsing, SWAP from discontinuous parsing) in a novel configuration for a new task. This is valuable engineering but not a disruptive conceptual frame. The transition set is well-motivated but not fundamentally new; each component exists in prior work.
evidence: NODE transition: 'we follow previous work in transition-based constituency parsing (Sagae and Lavie, 2005), adding the NODE transition'
REMOTE edges: 'node and edge transitions leave the stack unchanged, as in other work on transition-based dependency graph parsing (Sagae and Tsujii, 2008; Ribeyre et al., 2014)'
SWAP transition: 'as with the similarly named transition in previous work (Nivre, 2009; Maier, 2015)'
BiLSTM: 'an architecture similar to Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016)' and 'similar to Chen and Manning (2014)'
Contribution is solving a new task (UCCA parsing) by combining existing techniques, not introducing novel algorithmic or conceptual insights
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Reframe the contribution as 'first parser for UCCA' (which is accurate and valuable) rather than claiming disruptive novelty. Emphasize the engineering contribution and problem-solving aspect. Alternatively, identify and highlight any truly novel aspects (e.g., the ratio feature, the specific transition set configuration) more explicitly.

concerns.title: BiLSTM superiority confounded with feature representation and hyperparameter tuning
concerns.description: The claim that BiLSTM substantially outperforms sparse and feedforward classifiers is confounded by at least three factors: (1) feature representation (sparse vs. dense embeddings), (2) classifier architecture (linear vs. feedforward vs. BiLSTM), and (3) hyperparameter tuning (BiLSTM benefits from pre-trained word2vec embeddings and more extensive tuning). A controlled ablation isolating the BiLSTM contribution would be needed to validate the claim.
evidence: Section 3: TUPASparse uses 'binary indicator features', while TUPAMLP and TUPABiLSTM use 'dense embedding features'
Section 3: 'We additionally use external word embeddings initialized with pre-trained word2vec vectors (Mikolov et al., 2013), updated during training' (only for neural models)
Section 4: 'Hyperparameters are tuned on the development set' (same for all, but BiLSTM has more hyperparameters to tune)
Table 2: TUPABiLSTM achieves 73.5% vs. TUPAMLP 64.9% and TUPASparse 64.1%, but it's unclear whether this is due to BiLSTM architecture, dense embeddings, or pre-trained embeddings
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct controlled ablation studies: (1) BiLSTM with sparse features vs. BiLSTM with dense embeddings, (2) feedforward NN with pre-trained embeddings vs. without, (3) BiLSTM without pre-trained embeddings. This would isolate the contribution of each component and provide a fairer comparison.

concerns.title: No ablation isolating contribution of individual transition types
concerns.description: The paper defines 8 transitions (SHIFT, REDUCE, NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP, FINISH) but does not ablate to show the contribution of each. It is unclear whether all transitions are necessary or whether some are redundant. For example, is SWAP critical for handling discontinuity, or could remote edges alone suffice?
evidence: Section 3 defines all 8 transitions but provides no ablation study

Footnote 10 mentions: 'We also experimented with a simpler version of TUPA lacking REMOTE transitions, obtaining an increase of up to 2 labeled F-score points on primary edges, at the cost of not being able to predict remote edges.' This is a partial ablation but only for REMOTE transitions.
No ablation for NODE, SWAP, or other transitions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablation studies for each transition type: (1) without NODE (cannot create non-terminals), (2) without SWAP (cannot handle discontinuity), (3) without REMOTE (cannot handle reentrancy). Report F-score on primary, remote, and overall metrics for each variant. This would clarify which transitions are most critical.

concerns.title: Greedy inference without beam search or global normalization comparison
concerns.description: The parser uses greedy inference (selecting the highest-scoring transition at each step) without exploring beam search or globally normalized models. This may lead to error accumulation, especially for complex DAG structures with long-range dependencies. No comparison with beam search or global normalization (e.g., Andor et al., 2016) is provided.
evidence: Section 3: 'For all classifiers, inference is performed greedily, i.e., without beam search.'
Section 4: 'DAGParser and UPARSE use beam search by default, with a beam size of 5 and 4 respectively. The other parsers are greedy.'
No comparison of TUPA with beam search vs. greedy inference
No comparison with globally normalized models (e.g., Andor et al., 2016: 'Globally normalized transition-based neural networks')
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement beam search (beam size 5–10) and compare with greedy inference. Also compare with a globally normalized variant if feasible. Report the performance gain and computational cost. This would clarify whether greedy inference is a limitation or sufficient for UCCA parsing.

concerns.title: Dynamic oracle completeness only sketched, not formally proven
concerns.description: The paper claims to use a dynamic oracle for training (Section 3, lines 360–380) and references a 'proof sketch' in Appendix E. However, no formal proof of oracle completeness is provided. If the oracle is incomplete (i.e., does not always find a path to the gold graph), training will be suboptimal. This is a critical assumption for the approach.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 360–380): 'For training the transition classifiers, we use a dynamic oracle (Goldberg and Nivre, 2012), i.e., an oracle that outputs a set of optimal transitions: when applied to the current parser state, the gold standard graph is reachable from the resulting state.'
Appendix E: 'See Appendix E for a proof sketch for the completeness' (mentioned in footnote 12, but not provided in the manuscript excerpt)
No formal proof of oracle completeness for the UCCA transition set
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a formal proof of dynamic oracle completeness for the UCCA transition set, or cite a reference that proves it. If a proof sketch is provided in Appendix E, ensure it is rigorous and covers all cases (e.g., how to handle non-terminal node creation, remote edges, and discontinuity simultaneously).

concerns.title: Baseline comparison via conversion introduces confounds; direct comparison on UCCA would be more conclusive
concerns.description: The paper compares TUPA to existing parsers (DAGParser, TurboParser, LSTM Parser, etc.) by converting UCCA to bilexical graphs or trees and evaluating baselines on the converted representation. This introduces information loss (upper bounds: 58.3% for graphs, 100% for trees) and may unfairly disadvantage baselines. A direct comparison where baselines are retrained on UCCA would be more conclusive.
evidence: Section 4: 'As no direct comparison with existing parsers is possible, we compare TUPA to bilexical dependency graph parsers... To facilitate the comparison, we convert our training set into bilexical graphs.'
Table 2: Upper bounds of 58.3% for bilexical graphs and 100% for trees indicate substantial information loss

Results section (lines 612–615): 'While some of the DAG parsers' difficulty can be attributed to the conversion upper bound of 58.3%, this in itself cannot account for their poor performance on remote edges, which is an order of magnitude lower than that of TUPABiLSTM.' This acknowledges the confound but does not resolve it.
LSTM Parser achieves 69.9% on primary edges (in-domain), which is competitive with TUPA's 73.5%; the gap is modest (3.6 points)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: If feasible, retrain baseline parsers directly on UCCA (not converted representation) to provide a fairer comparison. Alternatively, acknowledge the limitation more explicitly and interpret baseline performance as a lower bound (due to conversion loss) rather than a true measure of their capability on UCCA. Discuss whether the conversion upper bounds are realistic or whether better conversion procedures could improve baseline performance.

concerns.title: No error analysis or systematic failure mode investigation
concerns.description: The paper reports aggregate F-scores but provides no error analysis. It is unclear which types of errors TUPA makes most frequently, whether errors are systematic or random, and how errors relate to annotator disagreement. This limits understanding of the parser's strengths and weaknesses.
evidence: Section 5 reports F-scores in Table 2 but provides no error analysis
No breakdown of errors by phenomenon (e.g., reentrancy errors vs. discontinuity errors vs. non-terminal errors)
No analysis of which error types are due to annotation ambiguity vs. parser limitations
No examples of common errors or failure cases
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide error analysis: (1) breakdown of errors by structural phenomenon (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal), (2) examples of common error types, (3) comparison of TUPA errors to annotator disagreement patterns. This would clarify which aspects of UCCA parsing are most challenging and where improvements are needed.

concerns.title: Discarded edges and nodes (inter-sentence, linkage, implicit) may be important for downstream applications
concerns.description: The paper discards inter-sentence edges (0.18%), linkage nodes, and implicit nodes during training and evaluation. While these are small percentages, they may be important for downstream applications (e.g., machine translation, semantic role labeling). The impact of discarding these elements is not analyzed.
evidence: Section 4: 'we adhere to the common practice in semantic parsing and train our parsers on individual sentences, discarding inter-relations between them (0.18% of the edges). We also discard linkage nodes and edges (as they often express inter-sentence relations and are thus mostly redundant when applied at the sentence level) as well as implicit nodes.'
Appendix B: 'further discusses linkage and implicit units' (not provided in manuscript excerpt)
No analysis of impact of discarding these elements
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze the impact of discarding inter-sentence edges, linkage nodes, and implicit nodes: (1) report performance on full UCCA (including these elements), (2) discuss whether downstream applications require these elements, (3) consider extending the parser to handle inter-sentence relations if needed.

concerns.title: Generalization claim to other DAG structures and languages is prospective and unvalidated
concerns.description: The paper claims the transition set 'will inform the development of parsers for other semantic DAG structures, and in languages that frequently use discontinuous structures' (Abstract). However, this claim is prospective and not empirically validated. No experiments on other DAG structures (AMR, SDP) or non-English languages are provided.
evidence: Abstract: 'its ability to handle more general graph structures will inform the development of parsers for other semantic DAG structures, and in languages that frequently use discontinuous structures.'
Conclusion: 'Our contribution to this literature is a general grammarless parser that supports multiple parents, discontinuous units and non-terminal nodes.'
No experiments on AMR, SDP, or other DAG structures
No cross-lingual evaluation (only English UCCA)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (1) provide empirical validation by parsing AMR or SDP with TUPA (with appropriate conversion of the transition set), or (2) reframe the claim as prospective and discuss how the approach might generalize. Alternatively, conduct cross-lingual evaluation (French, German, Czech UCCA) to validate generalization within UCCA.

concerns.title: Ratio feature contribution not isolated via ablation
concerns.description: The paper introduces a novel 'ratio' feature (ratio of terminals to nodes) as a regularizer for node creation. However, no ablation study demonstrates its contribution to TUPA's performance. It is unclear whether this feature is critical or marginal.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 350–360): 'Finally, for all classifiers we add a novel real-valued feature to the input vector, ratio, corresponding to the ratio between the number of terminals to number of nodes in the graph G. This feature serves as a regularizer for the creation of new nodes, and should be beneficial for other transition-based constituency parsers too.'
No ablation study removing the ratio feature
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide an ablation study comparing TUPA with and without the ratio feature. Report F-score on primary, remote, and overall metrics. This would clarify the contribution of this feature and its generalizability to other parsing tasks.

concerns.title: Inter-annotator agreement cited from prior work, not re-measured on current test set
concerns.description: The paper cites inter-annotator agreement (80–85% F-score) from Abend and Rappoport (2013) to contextualize TUPA's performance (73.5%). However, this figure is not re-measured on the current test set (Wiki passages 942–1028). It is unclear whether the inter-annotator agreement on the current test set is the same as the prior measurement.
evidence: Results section (lines 610–612): 'Its performance in absolute terms, of 73.5% F-score on primary edges, is encouraging in light of UCCA's inter-annotator agreement of 80–85% F-score on them (Abend and Rappoport, 2013).'
Inter-annotator agreement is cited from a 2013 paper, not measured on the current test set
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-measure inter-annotator agreement on the current test set (Wiki passages 942–1028) to provide a fair comparison with TUPA's performance. Alternatively, clearly state that the cited figure is from prior work and may not reflect the current test set.

concerns.title: Out-of-domain performance drop suggests domain sensitivity
concerns.description: TUPA's performance drops from 73.5% (in-domain Wiki) to 68.6% (out-of-domain 20K Leagues) on primary edges, a 4.9 percentage point drop. This suggests the parser is sensitive to domain shift. The paper does not analyze the causes of this drop or discuss domain adaptation strategies.

alternative_interpretations: The 'first parser' claim could be interpreted as a narrow engineering achievement (solving UCCA parsing) rather than a disruptive conceptual innovation. The paper's value lies in problem formulation and systematic execution, not in novel algorithmic insights.

BiLSTM's superior performance could be attributed primarily to pre-trained word embeddings (word2vec) and extensive hyperparameter tuning, rather than the BiLSTM architecture itself. A controlled ablation would clarify this.

The transition set could be viewed as a straightforward combination of existing techniques (NODE, REMOTE, SWAP) rather than a novel contribution. The novelty is in the specific configuration for UCCA, not in the individual transitions.

The baseline comparison via conversion could be interpreted as unfairly disadvantaging baselines due to information loss. A direct comparison on UCCA (without conversion) might show smaller performance gaps.

The out-of-domain performance drop (73.5% → 68.6%) could indicate that TUPA is overfitted to the Wiki corpus, rather than a fundamental limitation of the approach. Domain adaptation might recover some performance.

The generalization claim to other DAG structures could be interpreted as speculative rather than validated. The transition set is UCCA-specific (e.g., primary vs. remote edge distinction), and adaptation to other schemes is unclear.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about its limitations: conversion procedures, upper bounds, discarded elements, and out-of-domain performance drop are all discussed.

However, some confounds are not fully acknowledged: the BiLSTM comparison conflates architecture, feature representation, and hyperparameter tuning; the baseline comparison conflates conversion loss with baseline capability.
The 'first parser' claim is carefully phrased ('to our knowledge') but could be more explicitly framed as a narrow engineering achievement rather than a disruptive innovation.
The generalization claim is presented as prospective but could be more clearly labeled as such (e.g., 'future work will explore...' rather than 'will inform').
Error analysis and ablation studies are missing, which limits transparency about which aspects of TUPA are most effective.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper addresses a genuine gap (no existing parser supports the full conjunction of UCCA properties) and solves it through a well-designed transition set and neural feature representation. However, the innovation is primarily engineering-driven (combining existing techniques) rather than disruptive (introducing new conceptual frames). The lack of close analogs in the literature reflects the novelty of the UCCA parsing task, not the novelty of the algorithmic approach. The paper's value lies in problem formulation, systematic execution, and empirical validation, not in disruptive conceptual innovation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If TUPA's transition set were shown to be optimal (via comparison with graph-based or grammar-based alternatives), the contribution would be stronger.
If the BiLSTM contribution were isolated via controlled ablation, the claim of neural superiority would be more convincing.
If the transition set were validated on other DAG structures (AMR, SDP) or non-English languages, the generalization claim would be empirically supported.
If error analysis revealed systematic insights about UCCA parsing challenges, the paper would provide deeper understanding beyond aggregate F-scores.
If the paper introduced a novel conceptual frame (e.g., a new way of thinking about semantic parsing or DAG structures), it would qualify as disruptive. Currently, it is primarily engineering-driven.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes solid contributions to semantic parsing: it identifies a genuine gap (no parser for UCCA), proposes a well-motivated solution (transition-based parsing with novel transitions), and provides comprehensive empirical validation. However, the novelty is primarily engineering-driven (combining existing techniques) rather than disruptive (introducing new conceptual frames). The main concerns are: (1) confounds in the BiLSTM comparison (feature representation, hyperparameter tuning), (2) lack of ablation studies (individual transition types, ratio feature), (3) indirect baseline comparison via conversion, and (4) unvalidated generalization claims. These are methodological issues that do not invalidate the core contribution but limit confidence in the strength of the claims. The paper is above the acceptance threshold for a methodological venue (e.g., ACL, EMNLP) but would not qualify as disruptive novelty for a top-tier venue emphasizing conceptual innovation. Confidence interval reflects moderate-to-high confidence in the empirical results and engineering contribution, with lower confidence in the novelty and generalization claims.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents TUPA, a transition-based parser for UCCA that claims to be the first parser supporting the simultaneous conjunction of reentrancy (DAG structures), discontinuous constituents, and non-terminal nodes. The core claims are: (C1) TUPA is the first parser supporting this conjunction; (C2) transition-based approach with novel transitions is suitable for UCCA; (C3) BiLSTM substantially outperforms sparse and feedforward classifiers; (C4) 73.5% F-score is encouraging relative to 80–85% inter-annotator agreement; (C5) existing parsers perform substantially worse via conversion; (C6) transition set generalizes to other DAG structures. Evidence analysis reveals: C1 relies on 'to our knowledge' phrasing without exhaustive survey; C2 is motivated by conceptual similarity, not empirical proof of optimality; C3 conflates BiLSTM architecture with feature representation differences (sparse vs. dense embeddings) and hyperparameter tuning; C4 cites inter-annotator agreement from prior work, not re-measured on current test set; C5 uses indirect conversion procedures that may unfairly disadvantage baselines; C6 is prospective, not empirically validated. The paper's empirical results are strong and well-presented, but the attribution of performance gains to specific design choices is unclear due to confounded variables. The 'first parser' claim is supported by literature review but lacks formal exhaustiveness. The dynamic oracle completeness is asserted via 'proof sketch' rather than formal proof. Greedy inference is used without comparison to beam search or globally normalized models. The paper makes solid engineering contributions but lacks the controlled ablations and methodological rigor necessary to isolate sources of performance gains.
logical_argument_graph: UCCA exhibits three properties: reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes → No existing parser supports all three simultaneously (C1) → TUPA addresses this gap
Transition-based parsing succeeds in related tasks (dependency, constituency, AMR, CCG) → Transition-based approach is suitable for UCCA (C2) [ASSUMPTION: conceptual similarity implies suitability]

Three classifiers tested: sparse perceptron, feedforward NN, BiLSTM → BiLSTM achieves 73.5% F-score vs. 64.1% (sparse) and 64.9% (feedforward) (C3) [CONFOUND: feature representation (sparse vs. dense) differs across classifiers]
TUPA achieves 73.5% F-score on primary edges → Inter-annotator agreement is 80–85% → Performance is encouraging (C4) [ASSUMPTION: gap of 6.5–11.5 percentage points is acceptable]

Existing parsers adapted via conversion achieve lower scores → Conversion introduces information loss (upper bounds: 91% for bilexical graphs, 100% for trees) → Baselines perform substantially worse (C5) [CONFOUND: conversion may be suboptimal for baselines; no direct comparison on shared representation]

Transition set supports reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes → Transition set generalizes to other DAG structures and languages (C6) [ASSUMPTION: no empirical validation on other structures or languages]

concerns.title: BiLSTM superiority confounded with feature representation and hyperparameter tuning
concerns.description: The claim that BiLSTM substantially outperforms sparse and feedforward classifiers (C3) is confounded by differences in feature representation (sparse vs. dense embeddings) and hyperparameter tuning. TUPASparse uses binary indicator features, while TUPAMLP and TUPABiLSTM use dense embeddings initialized with pre-trained word2vec. No controlled ablation isolates the contribution of BiLSTM architecture from embedding initialization and hyperparameter choices. Footnote 2 mentions a linear model with dense embeddings performed worse than sparse perceptron, but this comparison is incomplete and does not isolate the BiLSTM contribution.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct controlled ablation studies: (1) sparse perceptron with dense embeddings vs. sparse perceptron with sparse features; (2) feedforward NN with sparse features vs. feedforward NN with dense embeddings; (3) BiLSTM with sparse features vs. BiLSTM with dense embeddings. This would isolate the contribution of each component (feature representation, embedding initialization, classifier architecture). Additionally, report hyperparameter sensitivity analysis to assess robustness to tuning choices.

concerns.title: Greedy inference without comparison to beam search or globally normalized models
concerns.description: The paper uses greedy inference for all classifiers (Section 3, line 340: 'For all classifiers, inference is performed greedily, i.e., without beam search.'). However, no comparison is provided with beam search or globally normalized models (e.g., Andor et al., 2016). Greedy decoding may accumulate errors, especially for complex DAG structures with long-range dependencies. Beam search or globally normalized models might recover 2–5% F-score, narrowing the gap to inter-annotator agreement (80–85%).

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement beam search (e.g., beam size 5 or 10) for TUPABiLSTM and report results. Alternatively, compare with a globally normalized model (e.g., using structured prediction loss). This would assess whether greedy inference is a bottleneck and provide an upper bound on potential improvements.

concerns.title: Dynamic oracle completeness not formally proven
concerns.description: The paper asserts that the dynamic oracle is complete (i.e., always finds a path to the gold graph) but provides only a 'proof sketch' in Appendix E (Section 3, line 380: 'See Appendix E for a proof sketch for the completeness'). If the oracle is incomplete, training will be suboptimal, as some gold graphs may become unreachable from certain parser states. A formal proof or reference to a complete proof is necessary.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 360–380): 'For training the transition classifiers, we use a dynamic oracle (Goldberg and Nivre, 2012), i.e., an oracle that outputs a set of optimal transitions: when applied to the current parser state, the gold standard graph is reachable from the resulting state.'
Section 3 (line 380): 'See Appendix E for a proof sketch for the completeness'
Appendix E is referenced but not provided in the manuscript excerpt; only a 'proof sketch' is mentioned, not a formal proof
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a formal proof of oracle completeness in the appendix, or cite a reference that proves completeness for the transition set. If a formal proof is not available, discuss the implications of potential incompleteness and provide empirical evidence (e.g., frequency of unreachable gold graphs during training) that the oracle is sufficiently complete in practice.

concerns.title: Baseline comparison via conversion introduces confounds and may unfairly disadvantage baselines
concerns.description: The paper compares TUPA to existing parsers via conversion procedures (Section 4, lines 540–580). Conversion introduces information loss (upper bounds: 91% for bilexical graphs, 100% for trees), and baselines use default settings without hyperparameter tuning on converted data. Additionally, baseline parsers use beam search by default (DAGParser and UPARSE), while TUPA uses greedy inference, making the comparison not controlled for inference method. A direct comparison on UCCA (without conversion) would be more conclusive, but this is not possible since baselines were not designed for UCCA.
evidence: Section 4 (lines 540–570): 'As no direct comparison with existing parsers is possible, we compare TUPA to bilexical dependency graph parsers, which support reentrancy and discontinuity but not non-terminal nodes. To facilitate the comparison, we convert our training set into bilexical graphs.'
Table 2: Upper bounds are 91% for bilexical graphs and 100% for trees, indicating substantial information loss
Section 4 (line 599): 'Default settings are used in all cases. DAGParser and UPARSE use beam search by default, with a beam size of 5 and 4 respectively. The other parsers are greedy.'

Results section (lines 612–615): 'While some of the DAG parsers' difficulty can be attributed to the conversion upper bound of 58.3%, this in itself cannot account for their poor performance on remote edges, which is an order of magnitude lower than that of TUPABiLSTM.' This argument is not fully convincing, as conversion may remove edges that baselines could predict.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge the limitations of conversion-based comparison more explicitly. Discuss which structural phenomena (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes) are lost in conversion and how this affects baseline performance. Optionally, tune baseline hyperparameters on converted data to provide a fairer comparison. Alternatively, implement UCCA parsing for one baseline parser (e.g., DAGParser) to enable direct comparison without conversion.

concerns.title: No ablation study isolating contribution of individual transition types
concerns.description: The paper introduces novel transitions (NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP) but does not provide ablation studies isolating the contribution of each transition type. It is unclear which transitions are most important for handling reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes. Footnote 10 mentions a variant lacking REMOTE transitions, but this is not fully analyzed.
evidence: Section 3 defines 8 transition types (SHIFT, REDUCE, NODE, LEFT-EDGE, RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT-REMOTE, RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP, FINISH)
No ablation study removing individual transitions or groups of transitions

Footnote 10: 'We also experimented with a simpler version of TUPA lacking REMOTE transitions, obtaining an increase of up to 2 labeled F-score points on primary edges, at the cost of not being able to predict remote edges.' This is mentioned but not fully analyzed.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation studies removing each transition type (or groups of transitions) and report performance on primary edges, remote edges, and specific structural phenomena (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes). This would clarify which transitions are most important and provide insights into the parser's behavior.

concerns.title: Ratio feature contribution not isolated via ablation study
concerns.description: The paper introduces a novel real-valued feature 'ratio' (ratio of terminals to nodes in the graph) that serves as a regularizer for node creation (Section 3, lines 350–360). However, no ablation study demonstrates the contribution of this feature to TUPA's performance. It is unclear whether this feature is important for UCCA parsing or whether it would generalize to other parsing tasks.
evidence: Section 3 (lines 350–360): 'Finally, for all classifiers we add a novel real-valued feature to the input vector, ratio, corresponding to the ratio between the number of terminals to number of nodes in the graph G. This feature serves as a regularizer for the creation of new nodes, and should be beneficial for other transition-based constituency parsers too.'
No ablation study removing the ratio feature
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct an ablation study removing the ratio feature and report performance. This would clarify the contribution of this feature and provide evidence for its generalizability to other parsing tasks.

concerns.title: Inter-annotator agreement not re-measured on current test set
concerns.description: The paper cites inter-annotator agreement (80–85% F-score) from Abend and Rappoport (2013), but does not re-measure it on the current test set (Wiki passages 942–1028). Inter-annotator agreement may vary across domains or annotation batches. Additionally, the paper does not analyze error types or systematic failure modes relative to annotator disagreement patterns, which would help assess whether the 73.5% F-score is acceptable for downstream applications.
evidence: Results section (lines 610–612): 'Its performance in absolute terms, of 73.5% F-score on primary edges, is encouraging in light of UCCA's inter-annotator agreement of 80–85% F-score on them (Abend and Rappoport, 2013).'
Inter-annotator agreement is cited from Abend and Rappoport (2013), not measured on current test set
No error analysis or breakdown of performance by error type
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-measure inter-annotator agreement on the current test set (or a subset thereof) to provide a more accurate baseline. Conduct error analysis to identify systematic failure modes and compare them to annotator disagreement patterns. This would provide a more nuanced assessment of parser performance.

concerns.title: Generalization claim to other DAG structures and languages is prospective, not empirically validated
concerns.description: The paper claims that the transition set 'will inform the development of parsers for other semantic DAG structures, and in languages that frequently use discontinuous structures' (Abstract). However, this claim is prospective and not empirically validated. No experiments are conducted on other DAG structures (e.g., AMR, SDP) or non-English languages (French, German, Czech). The transition set design is UCCA-specific (e.g., primary vs. remote edge distinction), and it is unclear how to adapt it to other schemes.
evidence: Abstract: 'its ability to handle more general graph structures will inform the development of parsers for other semantic DAG structures, and in languages that frequently use discontinuous structures.'
Conclusion (lines 700–799): 'Our contribution to this literature is a general grammarless parser that supports multiple parents, discontinuous units and non-terminal nodes.'
No experiments on other DAG structures or languages
Section 6 discusses differences between UCCA and AMR/SDP, suggesting that substantial modifications would be needed for other schemes
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (1) conduct experiments on other DAG structures (e.g., AMR, SDP) and languages to validate generalization claims, or (2) revise the abstract and conclusion to be more cautious about generalization. Discuss which aspects of the transition set are UCCA-specific and which might generalize to other schemes.

concerns.title: Discarded edges and nodes may be important for downstream applications
concerns.description: The paper discards inter-sentence edges (0.18%), linkage nodes, and implicit nodes (Section 4, lines 520–530). While these represent a small fraction of edges, they may be important for downstream applications (e.g., machine translation, semantic role labeling). Evaluation on full UCCA (including inter-sentence relations) might reveal lower performance.
evidence: Section 4 (lines 520–530): 'While UCCA edges can cross sentence boundaries, we adhere to the common practice in semantic parsing and train our parsers on individual sentences, discarding inter-relations between them (0.18% of the edges). We also discard linkage nodes and edges (as they often express inter-sentence relations and are thus mostly redundant when applied at the sentence level) as well as implicit nodes.'
Appendix B further discusses linkage and implicit units (referenced but not provided in excerpt)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the implications of discarding inter-sentence edges, linkage nodes, and implicit nodes for downstream applications. Optionally, conduct experiments on full UCCA (including discarded elements) to assess the impact on parser performance.

concerns.title: No error analysis or breakdown by structural phenomenon
concerns.description: The paper does not provide error analysis or breakdown of performance by structural phenomenon (reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes). It is unclear which aspects of TUPA are most effective and which phenomena are most challenging. This limits insights into the parser's behavior and generalizability.
evidence: Results section (lines 601–699) reports overall F-scores but no breakdown by phenomenon
No error analysis or discussion of systematic failure modes
No analysis of which transitions are most frequently used or which phenomena are most challenging

alternative_interpretations: BiLSTM superiority may be primarily due to dense embeddings and pre-trained word2vec initialization, rather than BiLSTM architecture itself. A controlled ablation with sparse features and BiLSTM would test this interpretation.

Baseline underperformance may be partially due to conversion procedures being suboptimal for baseline architectures, rather than fundamental limitations of those architectures. Direct comparison on UCCA (if baselines were retrained) would test this interpretation.

The 73.5% F-score may be acceptable for downstream applications (e.g., machine translation evaluation) even if it is below inter-annotator agreement. Downstream application evaluation would test this interpretation.
The transition set may not generalize to other DAG structures without substantial modifications. The UCCA-specific design (e.g., primary vs. remote edge distinction) may limit generalizability.

The dynamic oracle may be incomplete for some parser states, but this incompleteness may be rare enough that it does not materially affect training. Empirical analysis of oracle completeness during training would test this interpretation.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper addresses a genuine gap in parsing technology (no existing parser supports the full conjunction of reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes). The transition set design is novel and well-motivated. However, the novelty is primarily engineering-driven (combining existing techniques in a new configuration) rather than conceptually disruptive. The BiLSTM feature representation is incremental relative to concurrent work (Kiperwasser & Goldberg 2016, Dyer et al. 2015). The paper's strength lies in problem formulation and systematic execution, not in disruptive conceptual innovation. This does not diminish its value: it solves a real problem and opens a new parsing task.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the transition set were shown to generalize to other DAG structures (AMR, SDP) and languages (French, German, Czech) through empirical validation, the generalization claim would be substantially strengthened.
If controlled ablation studies isolated the contribution of BiLSTM architecture from feature representation and hyperparameter tuning, the claim of BiLSTM superiority would be more convincing.
If beam search or globally normalized models were compared with greedy inference, the paper would provide a more complete picture of the parser's potential performance.
If the dynamic oracle completeness were formally proven (rather than sketched), the training methodology would be more rigorous.
If baseline parsers were tuned on converted data or directly implemented for UCCA, the baseline comparison would be more fair and conclusive.
If error analysis and breakdown by structural phenomenon were provided, the paper would offer deeper insights into parser behavior and generalizability.
If downstream application evaluation (e.g., machine translation, semantic role labeling) were conducted, the practical utility of the 73.5% F-score would be validated.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes solid engineering contributions with strong empirical results, but the attribution of performance gains to specific design choices is unclear due to confounded variables (BiLSTM architecture vs. feature representation vs. hyperparameter tuning).
